introduction-you-are-the-product.core: In the job market, you are the product: skills are features, your résumé and profile are the packaging, interviews are demos and compensation is the price. Managing your career deliberately (positioning, evidence of impact, timing) beats waiting to be noticed.

first_principles.problem: Talented engineers stall because they assume good work speaks for itself.
truths: Decision-makers see summaries, not your daily work.
Evidence must be collected and presented.

analogy.title: A product launch
analogy.story: A great product with no marketing, packaging or pricing strategy doesn't sell.
analogy.breaks: Products don't have feelings; career strategy must also fit your values and wellbeing.

example.title: Repositioning for SRE
flow: Rewrite résumé around SLOs and MTTR

check.q: Why doesn't 'good work speaks for itself' hold?
check.a: Decision-makers see only summaries and evidence; undocumented impact is invisible.

resume-optimization-the-6-second-scan.core: Recruiters spend about six seconds on a first pass, and applicant tracking systems filter by keywords. Put the target title and key skills at the top, use reverse-chronological bullets starting with strong verbs and ending in measurable impact (XYZ: accomplished X as measured by Y by doing Z), and keep it to 1–2 pages.

first_principles.problem: A résumé lists responsibilities ('responsible for CI/CD') and gets no callbacks.
truths: Skimmers read the top third and bold items.

analogy.title: A newspaper headline and first paragraph
analogy.story: Most readers decide from the headline; the details must support it.
analogy.breaks: Newspapers can be sensational; résumés must stay honest and verifiable.

example.title: Rewriting a bullet
flow: After: 'Cut build time 45 → 12 min for 80 engineers by introducing remote caching and test sharding'

check.a: Accomplished X, as measured by Y, by doing Z.

the-star-method-winning-behavioral-inter.core: STAR structures answers: Situation (brief context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what you specifically did, the bulk of the answer), Result (quantified outcome and lesson). It keeps answers focused, around two minutes, and full of the evidence interviewers score.

first_principles.problem: Candidates ramble about context for five minutes and never say what they did.
truths: Actions and results are what's scored.

analogy.title: A well-told short story
analogy.story: Set the scene quickly, show the hero acting, end with the outcome.
analogy.breaks: Stories can embellish; STAR answers must be true and verifiable.

example.title: 'Tell me about a failure'
flow: T: I owned the rollout plan
A: I skipped a canary; I led recovery, wrote the postmortem, added mandatory canaries
R: 0 migration outages in next 10 rollouts

check.q: Which part of STAR should take most of the time?

negotiation-understanding-total-comp-tc.core: Total compensation = base salary + annual bonus (target %) + equity (annualised) + sign-on (amortised) + benefits like 401k match. Compare offers on TC per year across the vesting period, accounting for vesting schedules, refreshers, stock volatility and cost of living.

first_principles.problem: A candidate picks the higher base and loses $60k/year in equity and bonus.
truths: Equity varies by schedule and stock.

analogy.title: Comparing phone plans
analogy.story: The cheapest monthly price might hide fees, contract length and handset costs.
analogy.breaks: Phone plans are fixed; equity value changes with the market.

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: A's vesting is 5/15/40/40, so year 1 is lower.

check.a: Back-loaded vesting and one-time sign-ons make year-1 pay differ from later years.

the-brag-document-tracking-your-wins.core: A brag document is a running log of your accomplishments, impact metrics, feedback received and skills learned. Memory fades and managers change, so a brag doc makes performance reviews, promotions, résumé updates and interview prep fast and evidence-based.

first_principles.problem: At review time, an engineer can only remember the last two months of work.
truths: Memory is biased toward recent events.
Evidence must be captured when fresh.

analogy.title: A scientist's lab notebook
analogy.story: Results recorded at the time are trusted; recollected ones aren't.
analogy.breaks: Lab notebooks are formal records; brag docs are personal, but shareable.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Review self-assessment written in an hour.

code.text:
## Week 14
- Led Sev-2 response for payments; MTTR 25 min (runbook link)
- Mentored Sam on Terraform modules; Sam shipped first module
- Kudos from SRE lead on alert cleanup (-40% pages)

check.q: Why include 'glue work' in a brag doc?
check.a: Mentoring, documentation and coordination are valuable but easily overlooked unless recorded.

promo-packets-building-your-case.core: A promotion packet argues that you're already operating at the next level: evidence mapped to the level's rubric (scope, impact, technical complexity, leadership), backed by artefacts and peer feedback. Build it over months with your manager, targeting gaps early.

first_principles.problem: An engineer asks for promotion with 'I worked hard', and the committee sees no next-level evidence.

analogy.title: A lawyer's case file
analogy.story: Exhibits mapped to each element the judge must find.
analogy.breaks: Court cases are adversarial; promo processes should be collaborative with your manager.

example.title: Senior → Staff packet
flow: Scope: led cross-team observability platform (5 teams)
example.outcome: a promotion case that's hard to refuse.

check.q: What's the core argument of a promo packet?
check.a: That you're already consistently performing at the next level, shown with evidence against its rubric.
